opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a real tension, and I don't think there's a single right answer. It depends a lot on what the agent can touch.

The way I think about it is in terms of blast radius. If an agent is working in a sandbox, like a fresh container with a copy of the repo and no credentials, you can give it a lot of autonomy. Let it run tests, install packages, try things, because the worst case is that you throw the container away. That's where you get the big convenience wins, since you're not approving every little command.

It gets harder when the agent is connected to real systems: production databases, cloud accounts, your email, internal tools. One big mistake there can be costly or irreversible, so you want more structure. You scope credentials down to exactly what the task needs. You make writes go through review or some kind of staging step. You keep logs so you can see what the agent actually did.

Prompt injection is the other piece people underestimate. As soon as an agent reads untrusted content, like a web page, an issue someone filed, or a dependency's README, that content can try to steer it. So you can't rely on the model "being careful." You have to design the permissions so that even if it gets tricked, the damage is limited. That's the same principle we use for human engineers: least privilege, separation of duties, auditability.

From the data and platform side, a lot of what we've learned about governance carries over directly. You want the agent to act with an identity, with permissions you can reason about and lineage you can trace. If it's just borrowing your personal admin token, you've basically given up. If it has its own scoped identity and everything it does is governed the same way as any other user or job, you can be much more relaxed about letting it run.

So my practical advice is to be generous with autonomy inside well-isolated environments, be strict at the boundaries where it touches real data or the outside world, and invest in tooling that makes the safe path the easy path. If people have to choose between security and getting their work done, they'll pick getting their work done every time. The goal is to make that choice unnecessary.

r001.rationale: The response says that approving every little command reduces convenience, but it does not connect repeated approvals to the user's limited time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that most people are getting the tradeoff wrong in both directions at once. They lock the agent down so hard that it's useless, and then they get frustrated and flip it to auto-approve everything because approving each command one at a time is exhausting. Neither of those is a security posture, it's just friction fatigue.

The way I think about it is that the agent is a new kind of principal in your system, and you should treat it the way you'd treat a very fast, very capable contractor who you don't fully know yet. You wouldn't give a contractor your production credentials on day one, but you also wouldn't make them ask permission to open a file. So the question is really about scoping, not about per-action approval.

Concretely, that means a few things. Run the agent in an environment where the blast radius is bounded. A container, a sandbox, a scratch branch, whatever. If the worst it can do is mess up a clone of the repo, you can let it run freely and review the diff at the end, which is where review actually belongs anyway. Humans are bad at evaluating a stream of forty tiny permission prompts and good at evaluating a coherent pull request.

Second, separate the credentials from the agent. A lot of the scary stories are really about the agent having access to tokens it never needed. If it can't reach production, it can't delete production. That's an infrastructure decision, not a prompt engineering decision, and it's much more reliable than hoping the model behaves.

Third, and this is the part people underestimate, the data the agent reads is part of the attack surface. It will read a README, a log file, a web page, and if there are instructions embedded in there, you have to assume it might follow them. So the untrusted inputs should get the same scrutiny you'd give to untrusted code. We saw this with every previous generation of automation and it's no different here.

And then the convenience side is real. The reason these things are valuable is that they can run long loops without you babysitting. If your security model requires babysitting, you've thrown away the value. So the goal is to make the safe path the lazy path. Set up the sandbox once, give it narrow credentials once, and then let it go. That's the same philosophy we had with cluster schedulers and with data platforms. You don't make every job ask permission. You give it a resource boundary and let it work inside that.

Where I'd be careful is anything irreversible or outward facing. Pushing to a shared branch, sending an email, making a payment, touching infra. Those are the places where I still want a human in the loop, and I think that's going to stay true for a while. Everything inside the sandbox, let it run.

r001.rationale: It says approving commands one at a time is exhausting and that a security model requiring babysitting defeats the agent’s value, clearly presenting repeated manual approvals as a time-consuming workflow.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make the secure path convenient. If you give an agent unrestricted access to your machine and all your credentials, it can do a lot, but a mistake can also have a pretty large impact. So I’d start with an isolated environment where it can write code, run tests, and iterate freely, but has limited access to anything outside that environment.

Then you can put approval boundaries around things like accessing sensitive data or deploying to production. You don’t want to ask the user to approve every command, because they’ll just start clicking yes. You want approvals at points where the consequences actually change. That gives the agent a lot of autonomy for routine work while keeping the higher-impact decisions with the user.

r001.rationale: The response rejects approval for every command because users may start clicking yes, but it does not identify limited user time as the conflict.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make the secure path convenient. If you give a coding agent access to your whole machine and all your credentials, it’s easy to get started, but the consequences of a mistake can be pretty large. I’d much rather give it an isolated environment where it can run code, install dependencies, and test things without asking me about every command.

Then you put the boundaries around actions that matter: accessing sensitive data, changing production systems, or sending information outside that environment. Those are places where you want scoped permissions and, sometimes, human approval.

The other piece is making the work easy to inspect. If the agent produces a clear diff and runs the tests, I can review the result instead of supervising every step. That’s a much better balance than either giving it unlimited access or having it ask permission constantly.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes asking approval for every command and constant supervision, but does not connect that workflow to the user's limited time.
